output:
To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT - Brian's briefing for Embakasi casuals, Monday 30 November

Brian,

Here is the full position and a suggested run-through for Monday. I’m sorry you have to front this while I’m travelling. The main thing is that you are not going there to defend the company or face down the casuals. They did nothing wrong. We failed to pay them when we said we would, and management has asked you to apologise in person.

1. What actually happened to Friday’s pay

Casuals are paid fortnightly on Fridays. On Friday, Finance submitted bulk payment file TLL-CAS-2611B, covering 212 records, through the bank.

The bank rejected the whole file at validation. Column 7, the beneficiary reference, exceeded the permitted 20 characters under the bank’s new template, introduced after its platform upgrade on 25 November. No payment in that file was processed. Please do not tell anyone that the money left the company on Friday and was delayed by the bank. It did not.

The rejection alert went to the old finance mailbox. Kevin only saw it after 5pm, by which time the bank cut-off had passed. Kevin has acknowledged that this one is on Finance. It is reasonable to explain the bank’s new validation requirement, but do not hide behind the bank, the mailbox or the technical wording: we should have caught and corrected the problem in time.

Management has now approved making the payment through M-Pesa bulk B2C instead. Finance’s realistic estimate is that money will be on phones on Monday by 11am. Kevin has specifically said he will not promise an earlier time.

Peninah has checked the payment list against the phone numbers:

- 198 numbers are confirmed.
- 14 people could not be reached, mostly new loaders from the Athi River intake.
- Peninah will be at Embakasi from 7:30am with the printed list so those 14 can confirm or correct their numbers face to face.
- She will also have her laptop for anyone who wants a printed payslip.

Njeri has additionally approved KES 500 per person for Monday lunch and fare for every casual on the affected list, to be paid in the same M-Pesa batch. The M-Pesa charges are ours and must not be deducted from anyone’s pay. She has also asked for an in-person apology from management on Monday.

2. What you can say to the group

Keep the opening short and plain. Something close to this:

“Good morning. Your pay did not go out on Friday because the payment file we submitted was rejected and none of the payments were processed. The problem was found after the bank’s cut-off. That was our failure, not yours. You did the work and you were entitled to expect your pay on Friday. I am sorry for the delay, for the uncertainty and for the problems this has caused you and your families.

“Management has approved payment through M-Pesa instead. Finance’s realistic estimate is that the money will be on phones by 11am today. I am not going to give you an earlier or more convenient time that I cannot stand behind. We have also approved an additional KES 500 for each person on the affected list for today’s lunch and fare, in the same payment batch. The company will meet the M-Pesa charges; they will not come out of your money.

“Peninah will be here from 7:30 with the list. Most numbers have been confirmed, but 14 people still need to confirm theirs. She will also help with printed payslips. I will keep you informed rather than disappear after this meeting.”

If they say management previously told them “tomorrow” for three days, acknowledge it. Do not argue about whether that was this depot or a different supervisor. You can say: “You are right to be sceptical. That is why I am telling you exactly what has been approved, what is still being checked and what I cannot guarantee.”

Remember Mombasa in 2024: a supervisor said “by lunch”, the money arrived at 4pm, and half the shift sat down. We must not buy a quiet morning with another time we cannot keep.

3. What you can and cannot promise

You can confirm:

- The cause of Friday’s failure and the fact that none of those bank payments went through.
- The approved move to M-Pesa bulk payment.
- Finance’s realistic estimate of Monday by 11am.
- The additional KES 500 per affected casual for Monday lunch and fare, approved for the same batch.
- That all M-Pesa charges are being met by the company.
- Peninah’s presence from 7:30, the number-checking exercise and access to printed payslips.
- A management apology, which you should give without qualification.

You must not:

- Promise payment before loading starts, before the Kisumu trucks leave, by 9am, at 9am, or “within a few minutes”.
- Turn the 11am estimate into a guaranteed minute, or improve it because the yard is restless.
- Say the batch has been released, or that money is already on its way, unless Finance has actually confirmed that to you.
- Guarantee that anyone whose number is still unconfirmed will necessarily make the first batch. Their entitlement remains, but do not invent a separate payment time if their details miss the batch.
- Make payment, lunch or fare conditional on loading, or suggest that anyone who raises a grievance will lose the KES 500.
- Threaten dismissal, non-renewal, loss of contracts or blacklisting on Monday. The procedure expressly prohibits dismissal or threats of dismissal on the day of a stoppage.

If Finance gives you a confirmed release time or reports a further problem, pass it on promptly. Silence will do more damage than a difficult but truthful update.

4. The morning, including Ouma and the Kisumu trucks

You said you would be at the depot at 5:30. Start privately with Joseph before addressing the group. His report on Saturday evening was that the casuals were very bitter, some have rent due on the 1st, and Ouma and two others were urging people not to load the Kisumu trucks until they see money. The trucks must leave by 9am or we miss the offloading slot at the mill.

Speak to Ouma privately before the full-group address, with Joseph present if useful. Do not isolate him publicly or open by accusing him of organising a stoppage. He is loud, but he is not a bad man; he has rent and four children weighing on him. Those personal details are for understanding him, not for quoting back at him or embarrassing him.

Ask him to explain his concerns and what he has told the others. Acknowledge that “wait until 11” is not the same as seeing money, especially after previous broken assurances. Then walk him through the approved measures and the exact wording you will use with everyone. Ask whether, having heard the full position, he will help keep the discussion calm while you address the group. Do not turn this into a personal contest or a private bargain.

After the group address, allow questions without becoming defensive. Keep Operations working on the loading and dispatch plan in parallel. Do not wait until 8:55 to discover that the 9am departure is impossible. If loading is behind, escalate through the normal operational channel and warn the mill about the risk to its slot when the risk becomes real. A false pay promise is not an acceptable way to protect the departure time.

At 7:30, make sure Peninah gets a visible, orderly place to work and that the 14 unconfirmed workers can find her without disrupting the rest of the yard. Give the group a brief status update when she starts and again when there is genuine payment news.

5. If Ouma’s group still refuses to load

First, listen and establish precisely what they are refusing and what assurance they are seeking. Do not respond with a mass announcement about contracts, disciplinary action or replacement labour.

The grievance procedure says grievances go first to the shift supervisor and then to HR within 48 hours. It also says a work stoppage is not a grievance channel and must be handled by Operations and HR together. That means you should not treat it as an Operations-only confrontation. Involve HR immediately, keep Joseph’s account and the workers’ concerns in the discussion, and agree the next update with the workers’ representatives. Keep a factual record of what was said and agreed; do not compile a punishment list.

Keep people, vehicles and loading equipment safe while the joint discussion takes place. Operations can continue checking the trucks and the implications for the Kisumu slot, but no pay assurance should be invented merely to restart loading. There are to be no dismissals and no threats of dismissal on the day, and no contract threats on Monday.

If the refusal continues, keep the disagreement narrow and factual: the pay failure, the confirmed corrective action, the unconfirmed numbers and the expected timing. Do not accuse Ouma of acting in bad faith, and do not shame workers who choose to continue working or those who want more assurance.

6. Reaching me

WhatsApp me before I board if anything changes. I will be up from 4:30. My KQ flight leaves JKIA at 7:05, so please do not sit on a material change until after 7. If I am already airborne, do not wait for my reply before involving HR and following the joint Ops/HR procedure.

You do not need to win an argument on Monday morning. You need to apologise properly, give them only facts we can stand behind, keep the pay administration moving and prevent a bad payroll failure from becoming an unnecessary confrontation.
